The Objective, Its Gradient and Its Hessian, Stacked

Source: R/objective.R
statmod_objective.Rd

Builds the objective \(F(\beta) = -\ell(\beta) + \sum_t \rho_t\), which is not averaged over the observations, over the coefficients of every parameter stacked into one vector.

Usage

statmod_objective(
  spec,
  hyper,
  design = statmod_design(spec),
  expected = TRUE,
  approx = "opg"
)

Arguments

spec

A StatmodSpec().

hyper

The hyperparameters, per penalized term, held for the life of the objective.

design

The design. The function rebuilds it from spec when it is absent.

expected

TRUE for the expected information in he, FALSE for the observed one.

approx

How the expected information is approximated for a family with no closed form.

Value

A list with the elements

npar

the number of coefficients of each equation, an integer vector.

fn(b)

the objective at the stacked coefficients b, a single number.

gr(b)

its gradient, a numeric vector as long as b.

gr_sub(b, idx)

the gradient only at the positions idx.

he(b)

its Hessian, the information matrix (expected or observed according to expected) plus the Hessian of the penalties, a p x p matrix.

split(b)

the stacked vector as a named list, one entry per distribution parameter.

stack(l)

the inverse of split.

The objective is not divided by the sample size

A penalty is a negative log-prior at full size, and a posterior adds a log-likelihood and a log-prior at full size. Averaging only the likelihood would make a hyperparameter mean something that depends on \(n\).

Instead, the stopping rule is scaled, in the one place where it is read. See iwls() and iwls_score().

The closures share one design

The functions fn, gr, gr_sub and he close over design and hyper, and he also closes over the two information settings, so that a change of a hyperparameter requires a new objective. The outer search builds a new objective at every point that it visits.

See also

iwls() and fit_smooth(), which consume this, statmod_loglik_at() and statmod_penalty_at() for its two halves.
